chapter: New York arrival, Billy Hicks and the Black Cat
title: Skeets Talbot's band at the Village Black Cat
summary: Hall describes the six-piece band, the white clientele and John Hammond's sessions that began concert-style jamming.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Now, after you left Billy Hicks, you were with him a couple of years.
Then I went with Skeets Talbot.
I don't know too much about that band either.
Well, Skeets Talbot we had a band down in the Village called the Black Cat.
Oh, I've heard of the Black Cat, yeah.
And we were there a couple of years.
Oh, and let me add. This place was a converted garage, but the entertainment was black but the clientele was white. We didn't have any black clientele, and
They even did that in Harlem.
I remember hearing about the Black Cat or reading about it. Kenny Clarke played down there, that was afterwards.
Yeah, that's where Basie heard Freddy Green.

That's where John Hammond heard Freddy Green. John Hammond lived in the area on Sullivan Street and he used to bring his family to dinner. We worked seven days a week from seven to four, seven days a week.

Then what I wanted to say was that John was the one that introduced listening audience/concertwise. Prior to this it didn't happen, but he would come in and we had a small dance floor, and he'd have the waiters push the chairs out on the floor so he could sit and he would bring Benny Goodman, Harry James, the Count, Mary Lou Williams, Teddy Wilson.
No, to play, to jam. So that nobody would dance and I still say this is the beginning of concertwise jamming.
